title: 01. Fundamentals & Trade-offs: Availability
summary: Availability is the fraction of time a system is operational and able to serve requests correctly, typically expressed as a percentage of uptime (e.g., 99.99%) over a measurement window (a month or a year).
objectives: Explain the "9s table" and why the jump from four nines to five is so expensive.
Define MTBF and MTTR, and explain why modern systems focus on MTTR more than MTBF.
What is the difference between planned and unplanned downtime, and why does it matter for the availability budget?
What is a single point of failure (SPOF), and how do you eliminate one at each tier?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Availability is the fraction of time a system is operational and able to serve requests correctly, typically expressed as a percentage of uptime (e.g., 99.99%) over a measurement window (a month or a year).

Availability is the second pillar of system design, alongside scalability, and the two are often in tension. Where scalability asks "can the system handle more load?", availability asks "is the system up when a user reaches for it?" Operationally, availability is the ratio of uptime to total time: `A = uptime / (uptime + downtime)`. The industry shorthand is the "number of nines" — 99% is "two nines," 99.999% is "five nines" — and each additional nine cuts the allowed downtime by an order of magnitude. Two nines allows 3.65 days of downtime per year; three nines allows 8.7 hours; four nines allows 52 minutes; five nines allows 5.26 minutes. The jump from three nines to four is achievable with redundancy and failover; the jump from four to five requires eliminating almost every operational dependency, including planned maintenance, and is extraordinarily expensive. Most consumer systems target three to four nines; emergency-services and core-banking systems target five.

The "9s table" is the single most useful mental anchor in availability engineering. It translates a vague NFR ("highly available") into a concrete budget (52 minutes per year) that drives every architectural decision. Once you know the budget, you can answer: can I afford a single-region deployment? (No, if the budget is below ~8 hours, because a region-level incident typically consumes that.) Do I need multi-region active-active? (Yes, if the budget is below ~1 hour.) Can I afford planned downtime for upgrades? (No, if the budget is below ~30 minutes; you need rolling or blue-green deploys.) Can I afford a manual failover? (No, if the budget is below ~5 minutes; you need automated failover.) The budget also tells you how much to invest in observability — a system with a 5-minute annual budget must detect and recover from incidents in seconds, which means deep instrumentation and automated remediation, not a human paging through dashboards.

Availability decomposes into two underlying metrics: **MTBF** (Mean Time Between Failures) and **MTTR** (Mean Time To Recover). Availability equals `MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR)`. You can improve availability by making failures rarer (raising MTBF) or by recovering faster (lowering MTTR). In modern distributed systems, raising MTBF is hard — every component fails, networks partition, humans push bad deploys — so most availability engineering focuses on lowering MTTR. This is why chaos engineering, automated rollbacks, blue-green deploys, canaries, self-healing autoscalers, and runbook automation are so important: they shrink the time between a failure occurring and the system recovering. A system that fails often but recovers in 30 seconds can have higher availability than a system that rarely fails but takes 2 hours to recover when it does.

Real-world example: AWS S3's published SLA is 99.99% availability (52 minutes of downtime per year allowed). The 2017 us-east-1 outage is a case study in how even highly-available systems fail. An engineer executing a debugging playbook ran a command with a typo that exceeded its intended scope; the command removed a larger-than-intended set of server capacity from the S3 index subsystem. S3's index service was designed to handle individual node failures gracefully, but a large simultaneous removal triggered a metadata re-rebalancing storm that took the index service offline for several hours. The blast radius was enormous — S3 is a foundational dependency, so thousands of services that read assets, configuration, or even Lambda code from S3 also went down. The post-mortem lessons were architectural: (1) the index service had insufficient isolation between operational commands and capacity-removal logic; (2) the failure cascade was amplified by S3 being a hard dependency for so many systems (a lesson about dependency design, not just about S3); (3) recovery time was long because the re-rebalancing had to complete before service could resume — MTTR dominated. AWS responded with tooling changes (commands that exceed scope now require explicit confirmation), isolation changes (the index subsystem was re-architected), and cross-region failover tooling that customers could opt into.

Another real-world example, this time from Netflix. Netflix runs multi-region active-active on AWS — both US-East and US-West serve live traffic, and either region can carry the full load if the other fails. The reason is the 99.99% availability target: a single region cannot meet it, because AWS regions occasionally have multi-hour incidents, and a single region's incidents alone would consume the entire annual budget. Active-active also means failover does not require provisioning new capacity — the surviving region is already running at full capacity, so traffic shifts in minutes via DNS. Netflix invests heavily in chaos engineering (the Simian Army, including Chaos Monkey, Latency Monkey, and the regional Failover Monkey) precisely to verify that the active-active design actually fails over when needed, not just in theory.

Planned downtime is a frequently-overlooked component of availability. A system that takes a 4-hour maintenance window every quarter for upgrades is, by definition, not four-nines available — those windows alone consume 16 hours per year, far exceeding the 52-minute budget. The solution is to eliminate planned downtime via deployment patterns: rolling deploys (replace instances one at a time behind a load balancer), blue-green deploys (run two full environments, switch traffic atomically), canary deploys (route a small fraction of traffic to the new version, monitor, ramp up), and feature flags (decouple deploy from release). Database schema migrations are the hardest case — they must be backward-compatible and online, often using the expand-contract pattern (add the new column, dual-write to both, backfill, switch reads, drop the old column). Treating planned maintenance as a real availability cost is one of the markers of a mature system.

Pitfalls in availability engineering are well-known. **Single points of failure** — a single load balancer, a single database primary, a single DNS provider — invalidate all redundancy downstream. **Cross-region failover that has never been tested** — the design claims multi-region failover, but no one has ever actually run it; in a real incident, DNS TTLs, broken health checks, or stale replicas are discovered too late. **Cascading failures** — one slow downstream service exhausts connection pools in its callers, taking them down too, and the failure radiates outward. **Dependency concentration** — thousands of services depending on a single S3 bucket or a single Kafka cluster means one incident has massive blast radius. **Confusing availability with reliability** — a system can be "up" (returning 200s) but unreliable (returning wrong answers); both matter, but they are different metrics.

Availability connects to many later phases. Load balancing (Phase 5) provides the redundancy that underpins availability. Distributed systems patterns (Phase 6) — quorum, consensus, leader election — are how stateful systems stay available under partition. Message queues (Phase 7) decouple producers from consumers so a downstream failure does not propagate. Observability (Phase 11) is what makes MTTR short. Cloud regions and multi-region design (Phase 12) are the substrate for high-availability deployments. The art is choosing an availability target proportional to the cost of downtime, then designing each layer — compute, state, network, dependency — to meet it without over-engineering.

### ASCII Diagram
```
The 9s table (allowed downtime per year):

  99%       (2 nines) : 3.65 days
  99.9%     (3 nines) : 8.76 hours
  99.95%              : 4.38 hours
  99.99%    (4 nines) : 52.6 minutes
  99.999%   (5 nines) : 5.26 minutes
  99.9999%  (6 nines) : 31.5 seconds

A = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR)
        ^
        |  raise MTBF: fewer failures (redundancy, isolation, testing)
        |  lower MTTR: faster recovery (chaos eng, auto-rollback, runbooks)
```

### Walkthrough
1. Translate the availability NFR into a downtime budget (e.g., 99.99% → 52 min/year). Every architectural decision must respect this budget.
2. Eliminate single points of failure per tier: multiple instances behind a load balancer, replicas for state, multi-AZ for resilience, multi-region if the budget requires it.
3. Reduce MTTR via automated health checks, blue-green or rolling deploys, automated rollbacks, chaos engineering to test failover, and runbooks that an on-call engineer can execute in minutes.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
# Availability calculator and SLA budget helper.
# Translates "N nines" NFRs into concrete downtime budgets and
# shows the time cost of each additional nine.

def nines_to_availability(n: float) -> float:
    """99% -> 0.99, 99.999% -> 0.99999. n is the number of 9s."""
    return 1 - (10 ** -n)

def downtime_per_year(availability: float) -> float:
    """Returns allowed downtime in seconds per year."""
    return (1 - availability) * 365.25 * 24 * 3600

def fmt_duration(seconds: float) -> str:
    if seconds >= 86400:
        return f"{seconds/86400:.2f} days"
    if seconds >= 3600:
        return f"{seconds/3600:.2f} hours"
    if seconds >= 60:
        return f"{seconds/60:.2f} minutes"
    return f"{seconds:.2f} seconds"

def print_9s_table():
    print(f"{'Nines':<10}{'Availability':<14}{'Per year':<16}{'Per month':<14}{'Per day':<14}")
    print("-" * 70)
    for n in [2, 2.5, 3, 3.5, 4, 4.5, 5, 6]:
        a = nines_to_availability(n)
        per_year = downtime_per_year(a)
        per_month = per_year / 12
        per_day = per_year / 365.25
        print(f"{n}-9s     {a*100:.5f}%   "
              f"{fmt_duration(per_year):<16}"
              f"{fmt_duration(per_month):<14}"
              f"{fmt_duration(per_day):<14}")

def availability_from_mtbf_mttr(mtbf_s: float, mttr_s: float) -> float:
    """A = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR)"""
    return mtbf_s / (mtbf_s + mttr_s)

def sla_composite(slas: list[float]) -> float:
    """A system whose components are in series has availability equal
    to the product of the components' availabilities.
    Example: web=0.999, db=0.9999, cache=0.9999 -> composite=0.9988
    """
    a = 1.0
    for s in slas:
        a *= s
    return a

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print_9s_table()
    print()
    print("--- Series availability (web x DB x cache) ---")
    composite = sla_composite([0.999, 0.9999, 0.9999])
    print(f"composite availability = {composite*100:.4f}% "
          f"-> allowed downtime/year = {fmt_duration(downtime_per_year(composite))}")
    print()
    print("--- MTBF / MTTR analysis ---")
    # Rare failure, slow recovery
    a1 = availability_from_mtbf_mttr(mtbf_s=30*86400, mttr_s=2*3600)
    # Frequent failure, fast recovery
    a2 = availability_from_mtbf_mttr(mtbf_s=2*86400, mttr_s=30)
    print(f"rare+slow: MTBF=30d, MTTR=2h -> {a1*100:.4f}% "
          f"(downtime/yr={fmt_duration(downtime_per_year(a1))})")
    print(f"often+fast: MTBF=2d, MTTR=30s -> {a2*100:.4f}% "
          f"(downtime/yr={fmt_duration(downtime_per_year(a2))})")
```
